headline: Wall Street's AI rout deepens as Indian banks ride to record highs

segments.title: The big picture
segments.script:
Good morning. It's Sunday, the twenty-second of November, and this is your Market Brief.

Three things matter most this weekend. First, the AI sell-off on Wall Street turned into a rout. The Nasdaq 100 had its worst week since March 2020, and American markets lost around six trillion dollars of value in five days.

Second, India is moving the other way. The Nifty and the Sensex stretched their winning run to four sessions, and Bank Nifty climbed to a fresh all-time high.

And third, gold. The metal fell to a fourteen-month low on Friday, down nearly 10 percent in a single week. If you bought jewellery or coins this Diwali, we'll come to what that means in a moment.

segments.title: How markets closed
segments.script:
Let's start at home. The exact closing points weren't in this morning's reports, but the shape of the week is clear. The Nifty and the Sensex closed higher for a fourth straight session on Friday, and banks did the heavy lifting.

Bank Nifty jumped two and a half percent to an all-time high of around 64,600, with IndusInd Bank and Axis Bank leading. Livemint reports the banking index is up around 16 percent so far this month, with both public sector and private banks joining in. Brokerages point to healthy credit demand and strong lending pipelines.

Hospital stocks also had a good week, rising as much as 14 percent over five sessions. Apollo, Fortis, Max Healthcare and Aster all gained on Friday. On the other side, metal stocks such as Hindalco, NALCO, Vedanta Aluminium and Hindustan Zinc came under pressure as base metal prices fell.

Now to the money flows. Fund managers think foreign investors are turning friendlier. Raghvendra Nath of Ladderup Asset Managers expects foreign money to keep coming into Indian shares as long as the AI trade stays volatile. P Krishnan of Spark Investment Management is more measured. He says the buying is no big shift towards India, but the worst of foreign selling is over. And Jefferies strategist Christopher Wood has raised India's weight in his Asia portfolio to 15 percent, his second increase in three weeks, taking the money from Taiwan.

On Indian IT, Rajeev Thakkar of PPFAS Mutual Fund argues the market has overstated the threat from AI, saying four years is enough time for these companies to adapt.

The levels to watch. Technical analysts expect the Nifty to head for the 26,000 mark next week. A decisive move above it could bring a test of the record high of 26,373 from the fifth of January. For Bank Nifty, analysts see support at 63,500 and then 63,000, with resistance between 65,000 and 65,700.

segments.title: IPOs and deals
segments.script:
To the primary market, where the mood is cautious. The biggest issue in the market, Mahanadi Coalfields' 8,981 crore rupee offer, was still undersubscribed after two days. Its grey market premium has collapsed by 92 percent, to just 70 paise a share. Brokerages still like its production scale, cash flows and dividends, but investor demand so far is thin.

Two smaller companies have cut their plans. Medicap Healthcare, which makes pharmaceutical bottle caps in Vadodara, has trimmed its issue by 29 percent to 170 crore rupees and dropped a pre-IPO placement. And passenger mobility company Chartered Speed has cut its issue to 433 crore rupees after the market regulator's rule changes, with 333 crore of fresh shares and 100 crore offered by existing holders.

On the approvals list, the Securities and Exchange Board of India has cleared Pristine Logistics and Arohan Financial Services to launch their public issues.

In deals, TPG-backed Newquest sold a 115 crore rupee stake in Shadowfax, cutting its holding to around 6 percent from 7.35 percent. A Gallantt Ispat promoter sold 0.66 percent of that company. And the government's land monetisation company has eased terms on an 830 crore rupee auction of Hindustan Insecticides land in Delhi, giving buyers 240 days to pay.

segments.title: Results roundup
segments.script:
Results season is winding down, so this morning it's the sector picture. Public sector banks posted their highest-ever profit for the first half of this financial year, 1.09 lakh crore rupees, and their capital adequacy ratio improved to 16.89 percent.

Cement is the weak spot. Moneycontrol's analysis shows cement makers' profit per tonne at its lowest since early 2025. They are raising prices, but demand will decide whether that sticks.

Paint companies expect a better December quarter, helped by the shift in the festival calendar and the wedding season. Margins are still squeezed, though, because price increases haven't fully covered higher input costs.

And a note of caution from Raghvendra Nath of Ladderup, who expects December quarter results may not match the September quarter, and sees large companies best placed to do better than the broader market.

segments.title: Economy and policy
segments.script:
Now to the economy, and a strong number. Growth in India's eight core industries hit a thirty-one month high of 10.9 percent in October. Coal output rose 23.1 percent and electricity generation 21.6 percent, though both are measured against a weak October last year when they had contracted. Cement and steel also picked up.

Ahead of next week's GDP data, one Moneycontrol column expects growth of around 7.5 percent for the July to September quarter.

On the rupee, the Chief Economic Adviser made an interesting point. He said India may have to manage rupee strength, not weakness, next financial year, noting that several agencies expect Brent crude to fall below 80 dollars a barrel.

On trade, India and Canada wrapped up a sixth round of talks on their proposed economic partnership agreement on the twentieth. With the United Kingdom, there's a snag. The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence has applied an effective duty of 162.5 percent on bulk Scotch imports, higher than the 150 percent before the free trade agreement, and the Centre is working to resolve it. India is also the country most exposed to new European Union steel duties, with the bloc taking nearly 96 percent of its cold-rolled coil exports last year.

In Delhi, Prime Minister Modi challenged India Inc to show whether it has raised wages and created jobs after the tax cuts and trade deals. Food Processing Minister Chirag Paswan says the 40 percent goods and services tax on low-priced beverages is a concern and he'll push for relief. And ahead of the Budget, finance companies want a fund for lending to small businesses, managed by SIDBI.

From the market regulator, two consultation papers. One proposes scrapping extra ownership disclosures for certain foreign portfolio investors. The other tightens rules for directors of exchanges and depositories, lowering the age ceiling for public interest directors to 70 and capping a managing director's tenure at twelve years.

segments.title: Around the world
segments.script:
Around the world, it was a brutal week for technology shares. The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent over the week and dropped for a seventh straight day on Friday. The S&P 500 is on its longest losing streak since 2020 and has spent three sessions below its 200-day average, with traders watching the 7,200 line.

The trigger is worry about sky-high AI valuations, funding costs and whether data centre spending can last. Nvidia sank 14 percent after Reuters reported that US regulators are looking into its accounting. And Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, fell around 9 percent on its second day as a listed company, nearly erasing its jump from the 83 dollar IPO price.

The pain spread across Asia. Taiwan's benchmark had its worst week in thirty-five years, and regulators there have banned short selling below the previous close and say they've been buying shares. Chinese AI stocks have lost around 1.7 trillion dollars in value. Bitcoin slipped below 60,000 dollars, a two-year low.

One more from Washington. President Trump cited India's 7 percent growth to attack the Federal Reserve, saying lower rates could make the American economy grow far faster.

The week ahead is shortened by Thanksgiving in the US, but it brings the core inflation reading the Fed watches most closely, and a live debate on whether the Fed may actually raise rates.

segments.title: Your money
segments.script:
Finally, your money, and gold first. MCX gold finished Friday at a fourteen-month low of around 1,21,950 rupees for ten grams, while international gold ended near 3,539 dollars an ounce. That's a fall of nearly 10 percent in a week, blamed on a stronger dollar, talk of Fed rate hikes and the AI sell-off. Since Diwali on the eighth of November, gold is down about 12.9 percent. Silver has had it far worse, down around 65 percent from its January peak. DSP Mutual Fund says it is buying gold and silver gradually at set price levels rather than trying to call the bottom.

Now to tax rulings, three worth knowing. The Mumbai bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal has stayed an 8,520 crore rupee demand on the Government of Singapore, where the department argued investments through GIC were commercial and not covered by sovereign immunity. The Delhi bench held that capital gains on the transfer of a US entity by FireEye Ireland are not taxable in India under the India-Ireland tax treaty. And in Bangalore, the tribunal gave relief to a businessman in a 12 crore rupee case, allowing the seized cash to be treated as business income.

If you're parking money, company fixed deposits are paying up to 8.95 percent, led by Muthoot Capital, while NRE deposits for non-residents go up to 6.80 percent.

A warning too. A Bengaluru engineer lost 5.47 lakh rupees to credit card fraud without sharing his OTP or PIN, a reminder to set card limits and report unknown transactions at once. And banks will be shut on five days between the twenty-third and the thirtieth in different regions, so check your city before you plan a branch visit.

That's the brief. Today, watch for how markets open on Monday after Wall Street's rough week. The big tests are whether the Nifty can take the 26,000 mark, whether Bank Nifty holds above 63,500, and how the Mahanadi Coalfields issue finishes. Later in the week, the US inflation number will set the tone for gold, metals and technology shares. Enjoy your Sunday, and I'll be with you again tomorrow morning.
